title: The Serviceability Test Your Bank Runs Before They Say Yes to More Debt
linkedin:
A strong profit result does not guarantee a bank says yes to more debt.

We see this every EOFY. A business closes out a genuinely good year, applies for a facility increase or equipment finance, and the offer comes back smaller than expected, or takes far longer than anyone budgeted for.

Profit and serviceability are two different tests, and lenders only care deeply about the second one. Profit tells a bank the business made money over a period. Serviceability asks something sharper: after everything else is paid, is there comfortable headroom left to cover this debt, even in a quieter month?

Two businesses can report identical annual profit and get very different answers from the same lender. One carries little existing debt and steady cash flow. The other is already servicing a vehicle fleet, a lease and a line of credit, with revenue that swings hard by season.

The calculation is not complicated, and it is one an owner can run before any application goes in. Take EBITDA for the last twelve months. List every existing debt obligation, including scheduled principal, not just interest. Add the new facility at a realistic rate. Then stress test that headroom against a slower month rather than the annual average, because that is exactly what a lender will do.

A business that only just covers its repayments in its best month is carrying more risk than the P&L suggests.
